# Principles of cancer care

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Hematology and oncology > Basics of hematology and oncology > Principles of cancer care*

[Original Article Link](/library/TH06ph)

---

## Summary

Cancer is one of the greatest health care concerns for patients and their <u>health care providers</u>. An individual's lifetime risk of developing cancer is approximately 40% and cancer is the second leading <u>cause of death</u> in the United States. Once cancer is confirmed, further diagnostics to assess the <u>tumor grade</u> and <u>tumor stage</u> are required, and a comprehensive assessment of the patient (e.g., evaluation of <u>nutritional status</u>, social support, and mental health) should be performed. Treatment (curative or palliative) is based on the characteristics of the <u>tumor</u> and the ability of the patient to tolerate therapy. Cancer therapy may include a combination of <u>surgery</u>, <u>chemotherapy</u>, <u>cancer immunotherapy</u>, <u>radiation therapy</u>, and/or <u>targeted therapy</u>. Complications arise frequently as a result of cancer progression or as a consequence of cancer treatment; proactive management (e.g., <u>prophylactic antiemetic regimens for chemotherapy</u>) may greatly improve patients' quality of life. The majority of cancer treatment is managed by oncologists but all <u>health care providers</u> will see patients who have cancer as a comorbidity and should be familiar with common treatments, complications, and the need for <u>multidisciplinary cancer care</u>.




For details on <u>complications of cancer treatment</u>, see “<u>Complications of cancer therapy</u>” and “<u>Radiation injuries</u>.”

---

## Cancer-related complications

### Cancer-related emergencies




* Patients with cancer can develop life-threatening complications, e.g., <u>superior vena cava syndrome</u>, and <u>leukostasis</u>.

* See “<u>Oncologic emergencies</u>” for details on the diagnosis and management of these conditions.





### Cancer <u>pain</u> [[62]](/library/gXcFxa0)[[63]](/library/S8cyNV0)




* Cancer <u>pain</u>, caused by either the primary cancer, <u>metastatic</u> disease, and/or associated treatment, can be difficult to control.

* For further information including dosages, see “<u>Pain management in palliative care</u>.”





> [!TIP]
> <u>Pain</u> is undertreated in as many as 80% of patients with cancer; <u>assess pain</u> frequently, adjust <u>pain management</u> accordingly, and involve specialists early. [[62]](/library/gXcFxa0)




### Cancer-related fatigue [[64]](/library/5lcixc0)[[65]](/library/h8ccmV0)




* A chronic, distressing exhaustion that is severe, persistent, and not relieved with rest

* Occurs in approx. 80% of patients during <u>chemotherapy</u> or <u>radiation therapy</u> [[64]](/library/5lcixc0)

* Management [[64]](/library/5lcixc0)[[65]](/library/h8ccmV0)

* Identify and treat reversible causes.  [[64]](/library/5lcixc0)

* Blood tests: <u>CBC</u>, <u>inflammatory markers</u>, <u>liver chemistries</u>, <u>BMP</u>, <u>thyroid function tests</u>

* <u>Urinalysis</u>

* <u>Depression screening</u>, e.g., <u>PHQ-9</u>

* Encourage physical activity.

* Consider:

* Psychosocial interventions

* A short-term course of <u>corticosteroids</u> in patients with <u>metastatic</u> disease

### Cancer anorexia-cachexia syndrome [[66]](/library/ubcpva0)[[67]](/library/hf1cNT0)




* A syndrome characterized by progressive wasting of <u>skeletal muscle</u> mass with or without loss of body fat that occurs in patients with <u>advanced cancer</u> [[66]](/library/ubcpva0)

* Occurs in ∼ 50% of patients with <u>advanced cancer</u>; typically a sign of poor prognosis [[66]](/library/ubcpva0)

* Results from an excess of <u>proinflammatory cytokines</u> (<u>IL-1</u>, <u>IL-6</u>, <u>IFN-γ</u>, and <u>TNF-α</u>) as a result of <u>tumor</u> growth → ↑ <u>basal metabolic rate</u> and <u>catabolism</u> [[68]](/library/S-cy9U0)

* Clinical features

* Weight loss

* > 5% of total body weight in 6 months

* OR > 2% weight loss if ongoing and <u>BMI</u> is < 20 kg/m<sup>2</sup> or muscle mass is depleted

* Muscle wasting;  (temporal, deltoid, and <u>quadricep</u> regions) and loss of <u>subcutaneous fat</u>

* Decreased appetite

* Fatigue

* <u>Dependent edema</u> and <u>ascites</u>

* Management [[66]](/library/ubcpva0)

* Refer to a registered dietitian.

* Encourage oral nutrition; do not routinely use parenteral or <u>enteral tube</u> feeding in patients with <u>advanced cancer</u>.  [[66]](/library/ubcpva0)

* Consider pharmacological therapy to increase appetite and weight gain.  [[66]](/library/ubcpva0)

* First line: short-term trial of <u>progesterone</u> analog or <u>corticosteroid</u>

* Cannabinoid (e.g., <u>dronabinol</u>) use remains controversial.  [[66]](/library/ubcpva0)[[69]](/library/L5XwkA)[[70]](/library/o5X0OA)

* Provide psychosocial support to patients and their families.  [[67]](/library/hf1cNT0)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Cancer anorexia-cachexia syndrome</u> is an indicator of a poor prognosis.




### Cancer-related constipation [[71]](/library/NXc-ya0)[[72]](/library/HXdKzo0)




Defined based on the <u>Rome IV diagnostic criteria for primary constipation in adults</u>




#### <u>Epidemiology</u>




* 40–90% of patients with <u>advanced cancer</u> experience <u>constipation</u>. [[71]](/library/NXc-ya0)

* More common in patients receiving <u>opioids</u>





#### <u>Risk factors</u> for <u>constipation</u> in patients with cancer




<u>Cancer-related constipation</u> can be caused by the <u>malignancy</u> itself, other <u>cancer-related complications</u>, and cancer therapy; it is often multifactorial.




* Due to cancer

* Structural, e.g., abdominal masses, <u>peritoneal carcinomatosis</u>

* Neurological, e.g., <u>CNS tumors</u>

* Secondary to cancer

* Metabolic, e.g., <u>hypercalcemia</u>, <u>uremia</u>

* <u>Pain</u>, inactivity

* Poor oral intake, <u>dehydration</u>

* <u>Risk factors for primary constipation</u>, e.g., low fiber intake

* <u>Cancer therapy-induced constipation</u>

* Other <u>constipation-inducing medications</u>, e.g., <u>opioids</u>, <u>antiemetics</u>





#### Management




* <u>Nonpharmacological management of constipation</u>

* <u>Laxatives</u> [[71]](/library/NXc-ya0)

* <u>Osmotic laxatives</u>

* <u>Polyethylene glycol</u> (preferred) DOSAGE

* <u>Lactulose</u> DOSAGE

* <u>Stimulant laxatives</u> (may not be tolerated by patients who are weak or debilitated)

* <u>Senna</u> DOSAGE [[71]](/library/NXc-ya0)

* <u>Bisacodyl</u> DOSAGE

* Provide <u>treatment of fecal impaction</u> as needed.

* See also “<u>Approach to constipation in adults</u>” and “<u>Management of constipation</u>.”





### <u>Deep vein thrombosis</u> (<u>DVT</u>) [[73]](/library/KlcUBc0)[[74]](/library/6lcjBc0)




* Patients with cancer are at an increased risk of <u>DVT</u> formation, <u>DVT</u> recurrence, and bleeding during <u>DVT treatment</u>.

* Tailor management to the patient, including the type of cancer and <u>anticancer therapy</u>.

* See “<u>VTE prophylaxis in active cancer</u>” and “<u>Anticoagulation for DVT in active cancer</u>.”





### <u>Paraneoplastic syndromes</u>




* Cancer can cause a wide range of <u>paraneoplastic syndromes</u>, with symptoms ranging from mild to severe.

* See “<u>Paraneoplastic syndromes</u>” for further information.
